recoveryRoadmap.description: Step-by-step family recovery plan for the first 30 to 365 days after a death or severe incapacity. Use the steps in order and focus on documents, bank access, and claims before broader legal work.

intro.condolence: We are sorry for your loss. This roadmap is designed to reduce confusion and show what matters first.
intro.howToUse: Start with immediate documents and financial access. Then file insurance and benefits claims, complete legal administration, and rebuild the family plan.

startHere.0: Get certified copies of the death certificate and list every account, policy, and asset.
startHere.1: Pause or cancel auto-payments, subscriptions, and recurring card charges.
startHere.2: Review beneficiaries on life insurance, retirement accounts, and bank accounts.
startHere.3: Notify the employer, bank, insurer, and executor or next of kin about the death.
startHere.4: Collect original wills, deeds, IDs, and policy papers in one secure place.
startHere.5: Check whether there is a trust, power of attorney, or healthcare directive.
startHere.6: Keep a simple log of every call, claim, and appointment.

legalFramework.0: State probate and estate administration laws
legalFramework.1: Uniform Probate Code principles in many states
legalFramework.2: ERISA and employer benefit plan rules
legalFramework.3: Life insurance and disability contract terms
legalFramework.4: RMD and retirement account beneficiary rules
legalFramework.5: Federal and state tax return requirements for a decedent's estate

0.title: Immediate stabilization
0.focus: Secure documents, money, and legal records before the estate becomes complicated.

0.action: Obtain certified death certificates and keep at least 10 to 15 copies. Count them for bank, insurer, mortgage, hospital, and federal uses.
0.why: Every claim, transfer, and legal filing usually needs a certified copy. Missing copies create avoidable delays.

1.action: Review all joint accounts, beneficiary designations, and transfer-on-death accounts. Confirm which assets pass outside probate and which require formal estate action.
1.why: Some assets move outside probate because of beneficiaries or joint ownership. That is important for the first wave of access and protection.

2.action: Stop recurring charges: mortgage, auto-pay, credit cards, subscriptions, utility bills, and any small automatic payments. Ask the bank for a temporary review if needed.
2.why: Recurring charges can create late fees, damaged credit, and confusion during a family emergency.
2.legalRef: Consumer account terms and bank procedures

3.action: Arrange a safe place for original documents: passport, ID, deed, will, trust records, insurance policies, tax filings, and healthcare directives.
3.why: Originals often move faster than copies when a bank, insurer, or court needs proof.
3.legalRef: Document retention and estate administration practices

4.action: Notify the employer or retirement plan administrator about the death and ask about life insurance, disability, final paycheck, pension, or survivor benefits.
4.why: Employer benefits are often time-sensitive and may be separate from personal insurance policies.

5.action: Contact each insurer and ask for claim forms for life insurance, health insurance, mortgage protection, or disability benefits. Ask whether the claim is subject to a no-fault or contestability review.
5.why: Insurers often need the policy number, beneficiary designation, and death certificate before they can pay benefits.
5.legalRef: Insurance contract terms and state claims rules

6.action: Check whether a will, trust, or power of attorney exists. If there is a court-appointed executor or personal representative, ask for a copy and document all actions.
6.why: A clear chain of authority reduces delays and prevents disputes about who can act on the estate.

criticalMistakes.0: Not ordering enough certified death certificates. Banks, insurers, and courts often need multiple copies.
criticalMistakes.1: Assuming every account goes through probate. Beneficiary designations and joint accounts can bypass probate.
criticalMistakes.2: Paying off debts without checking whether a policy or benefit may cover them.
criticalMistakes.3: Using the deceased's online banking, cards, or passwords after death without authority.
criticalMistakes.4: Ignoring a will, trust, or healthcare directive because the family thinks it is not urgent.
criticalMistakes.5: Delaying employer, retirement, and insurer notification because the family does not know the plan details.

0.deadline: As soon as possible; state rules vary
0.consequence: Delay can slow down funeral arrangements, account access, and claim filings.

1.deadline: Usually within a few weeks to a few months after filing all documents
1.consequence: Benefit delays can make daily expenses and debt payments harder to manage.

2.deadline: Use the plan's deadlines and filing instructions immediately
2.consequence: Benefits can be missed if the family waits too long to file.

1.title: Claims and account transfer
1.focus: File benefits, move accounts, and identify what is probate vs non-probate property.

0.action: File life insurance claims, retirement benefit claims, and any employer death benefits. Include the death certificate, policy numbers, and beneficiary paperwork.
0.why: Many benefits are time-sensitive and separate from the estate process.

1.action: Move or close the deceased's bank, brokerage, retirement, and savings accounts according to the account terms and beneficiary instructions.
1.why: Accounts without a beneficiary or with a stale title often require formal administration before they can be transferred.
1.legalRef: Bank, brokerage, and retirement account rules

2.action: Review real estate, vehicles, and titled property. Confirm whether a deed or title transfer requires probate, a transfer affidavit, or a title office filing.
2.why: Property transfer questions usually cost time and money if handled late.
2.legalRef: State property and title transfer rules

3.action: Ask the bank or financial institution whether there is a small estate process, summary administration, or transfer-of-asset form available for the estate.
3.why: Some estates are eligible for faster procedures when the assets and debts are modest.

4.action: Document all debts, credit cards, and loans. Ask each creditor whether they have a death benefit, insurance, or debt cancellation process.
4.why: This prevents paying debts twice or missing benefits that belong to the estate or family.

5.action: Start the estate administration process if there is no beneficiary or if the assets require probate. Ask whether a will requires formal appointment of an executor or personal representative.
5.why: A formal court process can be important for property, creditor clearance, and family disputes.

mustHaveDocuments.5: Will, trust documents, and probate papers

criticalMistakes.0: Failing to file benefits before the family sees a bigger cash crunch.
criticalMistakes.1: Assuming all money can be accessed without checking beneficiary designations or joint ownership.
criticalMistakes.2: Leaving property title questions unresolved while the family is still grieving.
criticalMistakes.3: Paying estate debts or creditor claims before checking insurance or asset coverage.
criticalMistakes.4: Ignoring beneficiary updates on retirement and insurance accounts.
criticalMistakes.5: Waiting to open probate when a clear title or creditor process is required.

0.deadline: File as early as possible and follow plan-specific deadlines
0.consequence: The claim may stall or be denied if the family waits too long or misses required documents.

1.deadline: No universal deadline, but file promptly when probate or court action is required
1.consequence: Delays can increase conflict, cost, and legal risk.

2.deadline: Follow the decedent's final return and estate filing deadlines
2.consequence: Late or missed filings can create penalties and interest.

2.title: Legal and financial settlement
2.focus: Finalize estate administration, property transfer, taxes, and debt handling.

0.action: If probate is required, file the necessary court documents and keep a ledger of assets, debts, account activity, and distributions.
0.why: A clear ledger prevents confusion about what belongs to the estate and what has already been distributed.

1.action: File the final tax return for the deceased and any required estate tax or income reporting. Confirm whether the family must file as executor or personal representative.
1.why: The estate may still owe taxes, and the fiduciary has reporting duties. Missing these filings can create penalties and liability.

2.action: Review all loans, credit cards, mortgages, and debts and verify whether there is life insurance or benefit coverage. Do not pay debts blindly.
2.why: Some debt is covered by a policy or a benefit. Other debt remains the estate's responsibility unless it was jointly owned or a co-signer is liable.

3.action: Complete real estate transfer, utility changes, and vehicle title records. Confirm the deed, property tax status, and any mortgage or lien information before sale or transfer.
3.why: Title defects and unpaid liens can block a sale or create disputes later.
3.legalRef: Property title, mortgage, and local government records

4.action: Review healthcare directives, powers of attorney, and any trust terms. Ask whether the family needs to change fiduciary roles or update account mandates.
4.why: The family may need to replace authority on accounts, medical decisions, or financial operations after the loss.

5.action: Protect digital access: email, banking portals, cloud storage, social media, and subscriptions. Save and secure account records in a way that the family can use later.
5.why: Digital accounts often contain critical information and may require a legal process or collaboration with the provider to access safely.
5.legalRef: Digital account terms and privacy law

mustHaveDocuments.1: Inventory of estate assets and debts
mustHaveDocuments.2: Final tax returns and estate-related filings
mustHaveDocuments.3: Mortgage, deed, property tax, and title records
mustHaveDocuments.6: Digital account access list and recovery information

1.name: CPA or tax preparer
1.use: Final tax return and estate reporting

2.name: Mortgage or lender

criticalMistakes.0: Confusing probate with non-probate assets. The process is different for titled property and beneficiaries.
criticalMistakes.1: Failing to file the final tax return for the deceased or to keep the estate records current.
criticalMistakes.2: Selling or transferring property before the title and lien checks are complete.
criticalMistakes.3: Ignoring a trustee or fiduciary instruction in a trust or will because the family thinks it is optional.
criticalMistakes.4: Leaving digital accounts unmanaged after a death, which can lead to loss of records and access.
criticalMistakes.5: Paying debt without checking whether it was covered by a policy, benefit, or insurance asset.

0.deadline: As soon as practical when the estate requires court action
0.consequence: Delays can increase court costs, conflict, and administrative time.

1.deadline: Follow applicable federal and state deadlines for the decedent and estate
1.consequence: Missed deadlines can create penalties and interest.

2.deadline: Address early when a property transfer or sale is being planned
2.consequence: Unresolved liens or unpaid debts can block a clean transfer.

3.title: Rebuild and protect the family
3.focus: Protect the surviving family from future disruption by updating plans, beneficiaries, and emergency records.

0.action: Update beneficiary designations on all bank accounts, retirement accounts, life insurance, and investment accounts. Keep a written record of who is named and why.
0.why: Beneficiary designations are often the fastest way to avoid a repeat of this process for the next generation.

1.action: Review the family's existing will, trust, and healthcare plan. Update powers of attorney, executor designations, and emergency care instructions for all adult family members.
1.why: A valid plan reduces uncertainty when a family is under stress. Good planning is not just for older adults; it is for any family with dependents.
1.legalRef: Will, trust, and healthcare planning law

2.action: Build a liquid emergency fund equal to 6 to 12 months of essential household expenses. Keep it in a high-yield savings account or cash reserve rather than locked investments.
2.why: A family cannot manage a sudden crisis without accessible cash.

3.action: Review life, disability, and health insurance needs. Confirm that the surviving family members still have adequate cover for income replacement and healthcare.
3.why: Coverage gaps can create real financial strain later, especially when a household becomes dependent on a single income.
3.legalRef: Insurance policy terms and renewal rules

4.action: Create a single family asset register with account numbers, account types, passwords, document locations, and key contacts. Store one copy securely and share one copy with a trusted fiduciary or family member.
4.why: This turns a stressful crisis into a manageable checklist for the next generation.
4.legalRef: General recordkeeping and estate planning best practices

5.action: Review all legal and financial roles: executor, trustee, agent under power of attorney, and healthcare proxy. Make sure there is a trusted person ready to step in if needed.
5.why: The family should not learn mid-crisis that a role was never appointed or was outdated.

0.definition: The person named to carry out the terms of a will and handle estate administration.

1.definition: The legal fiduciary appointed to administer the estate under state law.

2.definition: The person or entity named to receive an asset or benefit on death.

3.definition: The court-supervised process for authenticating a will and administering the estate.

4.definition: A legal arrangement that holds assets for beneficiaries under the terms of a trust agreement.

5.definition: A document giving another person authority to act on your behalf for legal or financial matters.

6.definition: A document outlining medical preferences and who can make healthcare decisions.

7.definition: Ownership that may pass directly to the surviving co-owner without going through probate, depending on the jurisdiction.

8.definition: An account or asset that can pass directly to a beneficiary outside probate.

9.definition: A legal claim against property to secure a debt or obligation.
